To hinder someone or something means to make it harder for them to do something, move forward, or make progress. It puts obstacles, difficulty, or delay in the way — but it does not necessarily mean stopping something completely.

Think of it this way: imagine you are trying to walk forward, and someone keeps slowing you down by pulling lightly on your backpack. They are not stopping you entirely. You are still moving, but with great difficulty. That pulling force? That is what "hinder" captures.

The most important thing to understand about this word is where it sits on a scale:

Easy → Difficult → Hindered → Blocked/Prevented → Completely Stopped

"Hinder" lives in the middle. It is about creating friction and difficulty — not a full wall, but a serious slowdown. This is what makes it different from words like "prevent" or "stop," which suggest something is completely blocked. When something is hindered, there is still a chance of moving forward, but it is much harder.

"Hinder" is a transitive verb, which means it always acts on something — it always has an object. You hinder something or someone.

Two main patterns:

Pattern 1: hinder + noun/pronoun

"The storm hindered the rescue operation."
"His injury hindered him."

Pattern 2: hinder + someone + from + verb(-ing)

"Her lack of confidence hindered her from speaking up."
"The noise hindered them from concentrating."

Seeing a word in many different contexts is the best way to truly own it. Here is "hinder" across several real-life situations:

Physical situations:

  • "The thick mud hindered the soldiers' march through the forest." (The mud didn't stop them, but made every step a struggle.)
  • "Poor visibility hindered the pilot's ability to land safely."

Work and progress:

  • "A lack of proper tools hindered the construction team."
  • "Constant meetings hindered her from finishing the report on time."

Learning and growth:

  • "His unwillingness to ask questions hindered his learning."
  • "Anxiety can seriously hinder a student's performance in exams."

Relationships and communication:

  • "The language barrier hindered communication between the two teams."
  • "Mistrust hindered the peace negotiations."

Health:

  • "The pain in his knee hindered his ability to exercise regularly."

Notice that in every single example, the "hindering" thing is creating difficulty and slowing progress — but not always completely shutting it down.

Since learners often confuse nearby words, it is important to draw clear lines:

  • Hinder ≠ Stop/Prevent. "Stop" or "prevent" means something is fully blocked. "Hinder" means it is made harder or slower. "The rain prevented the match" (no match at all). "The rain hindered the match" (the match happened, but with great difficulty).
  • Hinder ≠ Help/Facilitate. These are direct opposites. To "facilitate" means to make something easier. To "hinder" means to make it harder.
  • Hinder ≠ Destroy. Hindering does not mean ruining something entirely. It means creating obstacles along the way.

When you use the word "hinder," you are pointing to something that acts like dead weight on progress — a force that drags, slows, or gets in the way. The hindrance could be:

  • A person (a rival, a bad manager, a noisy neighbour)
  • A thing (weather, poor equipment, a missing document)
  • An internal quality (fear, self-doubt, laziness, stubbornness)
  • A situation or condition (poverty, illness, conflict, bureaucracy)

Any of these can hinder progress, goals, movement, or people.

Since you are learning comprehensively, here are the word's other forms so you recognize them in the wild:

  • Hindered (past tense): "The bad weather hindered the team yesterday."
  • Hindering (present participle): "Stop hindering my work!"
  • Hindrance (noun): "His attitude was a hindrance to the group's success." (A hindrance is the thing that hinders — the obstacle itself.)
  • Unhindered (adjective/adverb): "She moved through the crowd unhindered." (Meaning: freely, without any obstacle.)
To hinder = to make progress, movement, or action harder, slower, or more difficult — like an obstacle that weighs you down without necessarily stopping you completely.
